utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-17/1-T, Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the accused hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This morning we are dealing with a motion raised by the Defence as a result of disclosure of documents by the Prosecution after the close of the proceedings. Now, I would like to state to both parties that the Trial Chamber has considered the motion and the arguments by the Defence and also considered the Prosecution response. At this stage, we do not find it necessary for further addresses except perhaps to give Defence counsel an opportunity for a very brief reply. Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I have just one moment to consult with counsel then? Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Our reply, we have read the Prosecutor's response brief. We obviously dispute almost the entire brief in its entirety, but in particular we make a strong objection to continuous factual statements in the response brief, particularly statements with respect to Witness A's mental condition, whether -- some of those include whether she -- let me find it in particular. They include statements like Witness A is not a schizophrenic, she is not delusional, she has no hallucinations. These are all factual statements. There is no affidavit attached to the brief, there is no reference in the record to any evidence to that effect, and so we would object to factual allegations or factual statements such as those in the brief that have no support through witness testimony at trial or any affidavit attached to the document. Our second and perhaps more important objection to the brief is that it fails to identify a single Prosecutor by name in the brief. We assume that the reference to a senior trial attorney and the use of a feminine pronoun to describe that attorney was a reference to Ms. Sellers. There is no affidavit from Ms. Sellers with respect to what her position was, why she apparently made the decision she chose to make, the document is not signed by Ms. Sellers, and I notice in court today Ms. Sellers is not present to answer any of those questions. We object to her failure to appear in court today on such a serious matter. That is our reply in short, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I notice that the Prosecution is different today. Who is appearing for the Prosecution, and may we also have an explanation as to why Ms. Sellers is not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Brenda Hollis and Michael Blaxill for the Prosecution today. Ms. Sellers is not here today. There was no instruction that a particular attorney be here today to represent the Prosecution, and I am here to present any oral argument or explanation that the Court may request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hollis, we see you are here and Mr. Blaxill is here. However, there are clearly serious matters to deal with here, and one would have expected somebody responsible to be here and present before the Chamber to answer to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could note on that as well that Ms. Sellers had scheduled a leave time after the conclusion of the case and had actually undertaken that leave prior to the filing of the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in future, the Trial Chamber expects that when serious matters of this nature, particularly regarding procedural issues in a criminal trial, particular trial attorneys should attend. You may be seated, Ms. Hollis. The Trial Chamber has observed that there was a serious misdirection on the part of the Prosecution in this case, in particular that Rule 66(C) does afford the Prosecution the opportunity to seek leave and advice of the Trial Chamber in camera in any matter where they have evidence or a document or anything that is relevant to the Prosecution of the case before the Trial Chamber where they are doubtful as to whether or not it is open to disclosure and that the Trial Chamber has got the authority to take a decision after inspecting the said document or examining the evidence which is relevant. In this trial, it is obvious that Witness A did receive either counselling or treatment as a result of the allegations which are the subject matter of the indictment against the accused before the Trial Chamber. So there was no question of the treatment or counselling not being relevant. It is clearly relevant. So the Trial Chamber feels that the Prosecution did not fulfil their mandate on disclosure, they failed in this regard, and the Trial Chamber is of the view that that did prejudice the right of the accused to prepare fully his defence, in particular in matters relating to a witness whose evidence more or less deals with the allegations, the subject matter of the indictment. Although the Defence in their motion are appealing to the Trial Chamber to strike out the evidence of Witness A or to order a new trial, on the second point, this Trial Chamber does not have jurisdiction to order a new trial. That is the premise of the Appeals Chamber. On the first point, on the first request that the evidence of Witness A be struck off, the Trial Chamber is of the view that this is a procedural error specifically in the hands of the Prosecution. It has nothing to do with an error committed by a witness. Therefore, the witness, in the view of this Trial Chamber, cannot be made to suffer as a consequence. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the best procedure under the circumstances and in particular considering the indictment in this case is to reopen the proceedings, allow Witness A to come forward for further cross-examination by the Defence, strictly limited to the documents in issue, the statement recorded by the Prosecution in 1995, for that matter, the Certificate attached, to allow the Defence further to call relevant evidence restricted to the issues regarding psychological or medical treatment received by Witness A as disclosed in these two documents. If they wish to recall Dr. Loftus, they are free to do so. If they wish to call any other specialist medical doctor, for instance a psychologist in this case, to deal with the matters raised in these two documents, they are free to do so. However, I must point out that the Trial Chamber is specifically limiting this reopening of these proceedings to the issues raised in these two documents. It is not an attempt to have a new trial, it is not an attempt to allow any party, either the Prosecution or the Defence, to call evidence which was not called at the time the trial proceedings were still proceeding. That being the view of the Trial Chamber, I would like to ask the parties if they have any objection or any further suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I should have discussed that in my reply because it was in their response brief. I cannot state, I guess, strongly enough how strenuously we object to the reopening of the proceedings for the simple reason that this was not a mistake made at trial, this was a mistake made well before the trial ever began. This statement was in existence since July of 1995. Mr. Furundzija came to the Tribunal, as you well know, in December of 1997, and the Rule says, Rule 68, "as soon as practicable." This is not simply, if you look at our motion, a matter of cross-examination of Witness A. The Defence made certain decisions which is what the whole Pre-Trial discovery process is for, to evaluate the Prosecution's evidence. That is why there is a sixty day limit in Rule 66(A) to provide the Defence with 60 days to prepare for trial, review the statements that are produced pursuant to Rule 66, and anything pursuant to 68, and then make your decisions as to, for example, Dr. Mujezinovic. Had we had this statement, his cross-examination can go into further detail. My questioning of him, let's say, what he knew, may be evidence that he could have given forward that would then have been relevant to any expert that we call is now out the window. In effect, it would be like trying to unring a bell. The bell has been rung, we made decisions at trial, we've made opening and closing statements, and in effect, to make a reference to poker, we put our cards on the table and now we're trying to go back and piecemeal as to how to reconstruct this. As you well know, a trial is not a piecemeal effort, it is one big picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the Trial Chamber has taken all those points into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You asked if we had an objection. That is our objection. I don't know that we can go back now and piecemeal try to reconstruct a case out of this. Secondly, the relevance of the statement is not just the statement itself, it is any evidence that we could have then, through investigation, have uncovered as a result of being made aware that she had a diagnosis as suffering from post traumatic stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what would you suggest, because the Trial Chamber has decided there will be a reopening of the case. So if you wish to recall, to have any of the Prosecution witnesses recalled, you should say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We haven't had time to discuss what we wanted to do with that because we didn't foresee that as a -- I mean, that was going to be part of an argument today as to -- we didn't foresee that as a fair or a possible solution to this because, as I stated, a reopening -- I hate to repeat myself, but a reopening puts us in a terribly awkward position now of doing things in reverse, in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. In that case then, you will be given time to reconsider the decision of the Chamber. It will be delivered in writing, and then you will be free to make any applications by motion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I make an oral application that in the meantime, to reconsider the ruling, since we didn't file a reply brief, didn't have an opportunity to file a reply, that would have been a significant part of a reply brief that we would file. I would ask the Court orally to reconsider the motion in lieu of what our stated position is and the problems that we are going to have in a reopening of the case. I stand here before you today unable to make a judgment as to this because I have to now look through the entire trial testimony, see how we can reconstruct this, but even at this point then, a reopening to us has created a sequence that is clearly out of joint and we have to see now what the effects are on the accused and his rights because we're conducting a cross of a Prosecution witness, potentially a reopening of the Defence's case in chief. Some of the witnesses, particularly Dr. Mujezinovic, may be relevant to us since he was a physician who examined her, he's the only physician whose name we have. We don't have the name of the witness who gave this statement. That has also been precluded from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If I may ask the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have one other comment that was given in a footnote that is particularly objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you conclude the psychologist known isn't it, from the submission by the Prosecutor . The one whose statement was taken by the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is known to us; is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the name and address can be given to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have not talked to the psychologist as to whether she would agree to that, so that was the reason that that was taken out at that time. It was felt that it was the substance of the information that was being disclosed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, if I may reiterate, it is not simply this witness that was, from our perspective, the violation of Rule 68. It is the Pre-Trial failure to disclose the issue that is the violation of Rule 68. It is the Pre-Trial failure to disclose the diagnosis, it is the Pre-Trial failure to disclose that she was having problems with memory. The fact of the matter is, at trial, we, if I may say so, basically had Dr. Mujezinovic not voluntarily offered that, we had no idea that Dr. Mujezinovic was a treating physician. We would have been entirely precluded from that entire area of questioning. Again, I draw the reference to unringing the bell. We can't tell you what we would have done had we known 60 days prior at least, but I say that Rule 68 imposes an even stricter requirement, what other avenues of discovery we would have pursued, what maybe would be different from my opening statement, my closing argument. It's not just a question of a particular witness, it's a question of trial strategy. It's a question of decisions made by counsel as a result of the evidence disclosed by the Prosecution. As you will recall in our last Status Conference, Ms. Sellers made on the record a statement that the Prosecution has fulfilled its obligations under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We were entitled then to say, "That is the entire Prosecution case, and we can then, as counsel to the accused, make decisions regarding trial strategy. So those decisions permeate the entire case, and again, I would ask the Trial Chamber to orally reconsider, if there is an alternative -- I mean, our belief is, at least under the common law, that striking the testimony is proper. It is not a punishment of the witness, it is a punishment of the Prosecution. The other point I would like to make is this is not the first time this is up. This is the fifth or sixth time I have been before you complaining about a misconduct on the part of the Prosecution. In my statement, in my argument, I was going to say: You, to your credit, have bent over backwards in this case to make sure that Mr. Furundzija gets a fair trial with respect to the issues previously presented, and yet to provide the Prosecution an opportunity to put on a case as pled in the indictment. We had the complaint filed by the Trial Chamber, then during trial, they tried to deviate from the indictment and we needed relief from the Trial Chamber to protect us from that. Now post trial we have even more problems. My position is, if this was the first time that this had occurred, perhaps the Prosecution should be given the benefit of the doubt. But on the fifth or sixth time, how many times must Mr. Furundzija come before you and say, "I have yet another example of misconduct on the part of the Prosecution." And as we go forward, rather than being smaller violations, they're greater violations. With all due respect to Witness A, her problem would not be with the Trial Chamber or with Defence counsel, her problem would be with the Prosecutors in this case and how they conducted themselves, and it's not -- shouldn't be a burden on Mr. Furundzija now to have to not have a trial as any other Defendant before the Tribunal would have a trial. Sixty day disclosure, time to prepare, here are the witnesses, put on your opening statement, cross-examine the Prosecution's witness, put on your case in chief, make a closing argument, and wait for the Trial Chamber to make a decision. Now because of their misconduct, he has to have a trial where the issues directly relevant to the case are now brought, in effect, post-trial, even though the Trial Chamber is opening up the proceedings again, disjointed, and in a way that I don't think -- I'm younger than Mr. Davidson but I would suspect that Mr. Davidson has never had to go through something like this in his 35 years and I certainly haven't had to experience a trial where we go out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I have 35 years. It's not uncommon in the United Kingdom if evidence emerges at the last minute, and after speeches, for the matter to be reopened. That is so. It seems to me that that is not necessarily an injustice or an unfairness to do that. While I am, as it were, speaking, perhaps you can help me with this: If you have the opportunity to cross-examine Witness A about the statement, if you have the opportunity to call any evidence about the matter or to have another witness recalled, if you wanted that other doctor recalled for the Prosecution, does that not cure any possible injustice or unfairness? I'm trying to understand the rest of the argument about your strategy. How do you foresee, how do you say that you're put at a disadvantage if the matter is reopened in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Because, Your Honours, first, to get to what I was saying earlier, we're not arguing alone that it's the statement or this particular witness that should have been disclosed, it's the information Pre-Trial i.e., this is a significant area that could have been and should have been developed by the Defence. That would have included witnesses that I can certainly say at this point in time, standing before you this morning, I don't even know their identities. So I can't say that calling Dr. Mujezinovic and calling Witness A back would cure the problem because it wouldn't cure the problem because a Rule 68 disclosure is an entire area. That's what I'm saying. The only reason we knew that she had psychiatric or psychological disorders, and I'm not sure that the distinction is that relevant at the moment, is because Dr. Mujezinovic testified as such. Now, the Prosecution states that in her 1995 statement, she stated she was suffering. She stated that she had physical problems, she suffered physical problems, she had rashes, et cetera, but there was no statement that "I have had psychological or psychiatric disorders," and indeed at the time she gave the statement apparently she was still going to Medica to receive treatment, not counselling as the Prosecution put it in their brief, it is treatment that she received. So, no, that wasn't disclosed to us. It should have been disclosed to us. We don't feel that it is a remedy to call one witness back or two witnesses back. On the second problem, which is, we've already put on a case before you. I can't say at this moment that maybe we would have made some other decisions that we wouldn't have called a particular witness or we wouldn't have pursued a specific area of questioning or we would have pursued a specific area of questioning with a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it does not do us any good going over what was not done, what was supposed to be done. We have reached the stage where there is a point, a good valid reason why the Trial Chamber has decided that it will reopen these proceedings, and that is a decision you have to comply with. When the written decision is handed to you, you are free to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's been our policy to try to go through the Trial Chamber to seek a redress before we go into an Appellate Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After due consideration of what the Defence counsel has submitted, the Trial Chamber is still of the view that the trial can be reopened, and that the Trial Chamber cannot order a new trial. However, in the reopening of the trial, the Defence will be free to recall any Prosecution witnesses, to call any Defence witnesses they feel like calling in order to deal with the procedural matter that has occurred in this case. At this juncture, I would like to ask the Prosecution what their views are, if they would need to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in terms of remedial action that would be appropriate in this case, we believe that the remedial action that has been stated by the Trial Chamber is the appropriate remedial action because it allows fundamental rights to the accused to confront evidence but it also enhances the overlying purpose for which the Trial Chamber is here, and that is the truth-seeking process, and does not punish the witness. Our opposition to the decision does not have to do with the remedial action, it has to do with the analysis leading to a decision that the late disclosure was prejudicial to the accused. The reason that we object to that is as follows: We believe that in making this determination, one cannot look to the documents disclosed themselves. Instead, those documents have to be put into context. And we believe that the context here includes the following facts: The statement that was taken by the OTP on which the Defence has relied in great part was taken in July of 1995, and in that statement, contrary to Defence counsel's assertions, this witness does indicate ongoing problems, effects, from what had happened to her, and she includes such things as the inability to sleep, the fact that she has bad dreams, she doesn't want to sleep. So she's not just talking about physical symptoms, she's talking about the psychological impact of the trauma. The disclosed documents are in July of 1995 and in September of 1995. So they are talking about the same time frame. They do not add anything significant to what is in the OTP statement. The fact that they add a label to the symptoms that are in the OTP statement do not give greater validity or concern to those symptoms, and the Defence was fully aware of the OTP statement and her description in that statement of psychological as well as physical effects of what had happened to her. In addition to that, Your Honour, the Defence was aware that this witness had gone to Medica and had received counselling, and we suggest it is a distinction with no difference to say it was counselling, not treatment, because counselling, for most purposes, in fact perhaps for all purposes, is treatment. And if we look at the Defence submission itself, we suggest it becomes clear that there was, in fact, no prejudice for this late disclosure. If you look at the discussion by the Defence where they say that the late disclosure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, may I interrupt you? It is not the intention of this Trial Chamber to ask you to repeat what has been submitted in writing already. I was just asking the Prosecution that, in view of the order by the Trial Chamber to reopen, is there anything the Prosecution wishes to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I thought you also asked if we had any opposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then if we're not allowed to state any further our opposition, we have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic, you have understood the order of the Trial Chamber as to the reopening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: A written decision will be issued, and you are free to take your decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has got other ongoing trials, and it is our view that in reopening this trial, we are looking at six weeks' time. We would be happy to schedule the first hearing on the 31st August, which is a Monday, and perhaps going to the second day, which is the 1st of September. So those are the dates the Trial Chamber is looking at, and the Trial Chamber believes that both parties have sufficient time to prepare their cases soon after the written decision of the Trial Chamber has been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for the following remedy also in the order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That the Prosecution be required to disclose any additional information with respect to psychological or psychiatric care or treatment? The brief they filed is very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It only answers the Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It uses terms like there is no evidence that she underwent psychiatric treatment at Medica. It never comes out and says there is no evidence that she underwent psychiatric treatment or had any disorders, period. What I am concerned with is I don't feel like coming back in the middle of September when potentially more evidence is disclosed even after this, so if we could, to use the phrase, an ounce of prevention -- whatever. You know the statement. I would prefer to know that in advance if the Trial Chamber agrees with the Defence that in light of your ruling today, that it is a relevant area and if they do have more in their files with respect to this area, perhaps it might expedite our investigative efforts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You have understood what Mr. Misetic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The reference to psychiatric care by Medica was a direct response to the Defence pleading, it was not an attempt to, if you will, use fine distinctions to hide any sort of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I ask this question then: Is there any other evidence that the Prosecution have regarding treatment, psychological or medical or counselling, on Witness A as a result of the trauma she underwent as a result of the allegations, the subject matter of the indictment against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I consult for a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. After consultation with co-counsel, the Prosecutor at this time is not aware of additional evidence. Because of the sensitivity of this issue, we will certainly undertake yet another search to ensure that, but at this time, we are not aware of additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have come to the end of our proceedings in this matter. We shall adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: sine die at 9.37 a.m.
